documents.unit: Instructional Design and Delivery (AI in Higher Education)
documents.title: AI Guides and Resources for Students: Asking the Right Questions: A Student Guide to Responsible AI Use in College
documents.summary: A student guide urging reflective AI use. It says each instructor sets the rules, tells students to ask when unsure, to be honest about use, and warns that over-reliance undermines learning.
documents.stance_why: The guide states "Each faculty member sets their own expectations for AI use in their course" and tells students to "Always ask if you’re unsure", so it sets no stance and defers to instructors.

units.why: The guide says "Each faculty member sets their own expectations for AI use in their course." This hands the AI decision to each instructor, so P04 (instructor sets the rule), addressed to all and informing students.
units.anchor: Each faculty member sets their own expectations for AI use in their course.

units.why: "Some may permit it in limited ways; others may prohibit it entirely" describes the range of instructor rules. It states variation across courses, not a tier system, so P04 and not P05.
units.anchor: Some may permit it in limited ways; others may prohibit it entirely.

units.why: "Always ask if you’re unsure" tells students to ask the instructor when they do not know the rule. That matches P10.
units.anchor: Always ask if you’re unsure.

units.why: "While AI tools can be helpful, relying on them too heavily can hinder your personal growth" explains why heavy reliance is cautioned. It is a learning rationale, so P41 (AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill), informing.
units.anchor: relying on them too heavily can hinder your personal growth
units.frag_start: While AI tools can be helpful

units.why: "When AI writes your arguments, solves your problems, or reflects for you, it undermines the very skills" states that outsourcing work to AI undermines skill. This is the P41 rationale and not a rule (P19), since it forbids nothing explicitly.
units.anchor: When AI writes your arguments, solves your problems, or reflects for you
units.policy: When AI writes your arguments, solves your problems, or reflects for you, it undermines the very skills students are at Gonzaga to build.

units.why: "Am I using AI to enhance my learning, or to replace it?" is a self-check prompt telling students to keep AI from replacing their own learning, which is P32 (student stays primary problem-solver); phrased as a question so modality is should.
units.anchor: Am I using AI to enhance my learning, or to replace it?
units.frag_start: Am I using AI to enhance
units.policy: Students ask themselves whether they are using AI to enhance their learning or to replace it.

units.why: "Does this use of AI reflect my own voice, ideas and values?" asks students to check that work is their own. P29 (own what you submit) fits best; P32 is about who does the problem-solving.
units.anchor: Does this use of AI reflect my own voice, ideas and values?
units.frag_start: Does this use of AI reflect
units.policy: Students ask themselves whether a use of AI reflects their own voice, ideas and values.

units.why: "Don’t assume any AI use is acceptable" sets a default for silence: no assumption of permission. That is a fallback (P06), not the ask-first advice coded separately as P10.
units.anchor: Don’t assume any AI use is acceptable.

units.why: "If AI use isn’t clearly addressed by the professor or course syllabus, have a conversation with your instructor" tells unsure students to ask. P10 fits.
units.anchor: have a conversation with your instructor
units.frag_start: If AI use isn’t clearly addressed
units.policy: If AI use is not clearly addressed by the professor or course syllabus, students have a conversation with their instructor.

units.why: "Work with faculty to understand when and how AI can support (but not replace) your voice" says AI may support but not replace the student’s own voice, with faculty deciding. P32 fits (AI must not replace thinking).
units.anchor: when and how AI can support (but not replace) your voice

units.why: "What counts as academic dishonesty can vary by course" warns that rules differ between courses, so one course’s allowance does not carry over. This matches P11.
units.anchor: What counts as academic dishonesty can vary by course.

units.why: "always be honest and clear about how you’ve used AI in your work" is a baseline disclosure expectation, so P24, with should since it is phrased as a baseline.
units.anchor: always be honest and clear about how you’ve used AI in your work
units.frag_start: As a baseline, always be honest

units.why: "Learning requires struggle sometimes. Ask where AI could get in the way of your growth." gives productive struggle as the reason to ask where AI is off-limits. P41 fits.
units.anchor: Learning requires struggle sometimes.
units.frag_end: get in the way of your growth.

units.why: "Using AI responsibly doesn’t just mean avoiding plagiarism, it means making choices that help you become the learner" states a principle for AI use at the university, so P56 (framework/principles).
units.anchor: Using AI responsibly doesn’t just mean avoiding plagiarism
units.frag_start: Using AI responsibly doesn’t just mean

units.why: "Gonzaga University provides clear guidelines to help students navigate the responsible use of artificial intelligence" introduces the IT guidelines as the institutional framework, so P56.
units.anchor: Gonzaga University provides clear guidelines to help students navigate the responsible use

documents.unit: Information Technology Services / Office of Information Security
documents.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Guidelines
documents.summary: Information-security guidelines for the whole community. They list approved and unapproved AI tools for university data, give privacy and verification advice, mention bias, and include a glossary.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule on whether students may use AI for coursework; its rules concern which tools may be used with Gonzaga data ("Approved AI List"), so it sets no academic-use stance.

units.why: "committed to providing guidance on the ethical and responsible use of generative Artificial Intelligence" states the office’s purpose, so a framework statement (P56).
units.anchor: committed to providing guidance on the ethical and responsible use of generative Artificial Intelligence

units.why: "our guidelines will continue to evolve" says the guidelines are provisional, so P54.
units.anchor: our guidelines will continue to evolve
units.frag_start: As Gonzaga University advances its integration

units.why: "We urge caution when using external AI systems, as they may not offer the same level of security and privacy" is advice on privacy and tool choice, so P50, with should and a restrictive lean.
units.anchor: We urge caution when using external AI systems
units.policy: The university urges caution when using external AI systems, as they may not offer the same level of security and privacy as AI systems managed by the University.

units.why: "Sandboxed means that the company/org will not use data uploaded into their AI training model" defines a term that sets what the approved list covers, so P61.
units.anchor: Sandboxed means that the company/org will not use data uploaded into their AI training model.

units.why: "Lower paid tiers and free tiers are usually NOT sandboxed" is a fact about which tool tiers protect data, supporting P50 (vetted tools).
units.anchor: Lower paid tiers and free tiers are usually NOT sandboxed.

units.why: Use of AI tools with Gonzaga data "must be made with an AI tool that has been fully approved" through contract review. A binding rule to use vetted tools, so P50 (not P65, which is about the institution’s review).
units.anchor: fully approved through Gonzaga’s vendor integration contract review process
units.frag_start: The use of the AI tools with Gonzaga data
units.policy: The use of AI tools with Gonzaga data must be made with an AI tool that has been fully approved through Gonzaga’s vendor integration contract review process, resulting in a business data sharing agreement, and that is managed by ITS.

units.why: The approved list marks "Microsoft Copilot (when logged in using Gonzaga SSO)" with a check, so it may be used with Gonzaga data. A list of vetted tools is P50.
units.anchor: Microsoft Copilot (when logged in using Gonzaga SSO)
units.policy: Microsoft Copilot, when logged in using Gonzaga SSO, is approved for use with Gonzaga University data.

units.why: Gemini, NotebookLM and Consensus are marked approved when logged in using Gonzaga SSO. Same type as the Copilot entry, P50 (vetted tools).
units.anchor: Gemini (when logged in using Gonzaga SSO)
units.policy: Gemini, NotebookLM and Consensus, when logged in using Gonzaga SSO, are approved for use with Gonzaga University data.

units.why: ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Otter and unapproved Copilot are marked not approved, so they cannot be used with Gonzaga data. A restriction on tools for data protection, P50.
units.anchor: All other NON-sandboxed AI
units.policy: ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Otter, Microsoft Copilot when not logged in using Gonzaga SSO, and all other non-sandboxed AI are not approved for use with Gonzaga University data.

units.why: "The restrictions above only apply to data covered by Gonzaga's IT Use Policy" limits the scope of the approved-tools rules, so P61.
units.anchor: The restrictions above only apply to data covered by Gonzaga's IT Use Policy.

units.why: Sensitive data such as PII and PHI "should not be uploaded or processed on platforms not approved". This is a data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: should not be uploaded or processed on platforms not approved on the previous list

units.why: "Generative AIs often integrate all input they receive, including prompts" explains why data should be protected: AI tools keep prompts. That is P50.
units.anchor: Generative AIs often integrate all input they receive, including prompts
units.frag_start: Generative AIs often integrate all input

units.why: "You should only provide prompts and other data meant for public sharing" limits what users put into AI tools, P50.
units.anchor: You should only provide prompts and other data meant for public sharing.

units.why: "varying degrees of respect for authorial rights among providers" raises the rights of authors in training data, so P52.
units.anchor: varying degrees of respect for authorial rights among providers
units.frag_start: Generative AIs also collect extensive data

units.why: "they can sometimes yield inaccurate information that appears credible, potentially fabricating sources" says AI output can be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: they can sometimes yield inaccurate information that appears credible
units.frag_start: Generative AI systems create text by forecasting

units.why: "It is essential to verify the accuracy of any information utilized" tells users to verify AI output, P31. Modality should since the verb is "essential" without a command form.
units.anchor: It is essential to verify the accuracy of any information utilized.

units.why: "Generative AIs mirror and can magnify biases embedded within their training datasets" names bias as a harm, P53.
units.anchor: Generative AIs mirror and can magnify biases embedded within their training datasets.
units.frag_start: Generative AIs mirror and can magnify

units.why: "We encourage our community to approach AI with a discerning mindset, advocating truth, equity, and the common good" states a guiding principle, P56.
units.anchor: We encourage our community to approach AI with a discerning mindset
units.frag_start: We encourage our community to approach AI

units.why: The glossary defines "Artificial Intelligence" as "a super-smart computer system that can imitate humans in some ways". A definition setting terms, P61.
units.anchor: Artificial intelligence is basically a super-smart computer system that can imitate humans in some ways

units.why: The glossary defines generative AI: "leverages the power of large language models to make new things". Definition, P61.
units.anchor: Generative AI leverages the power of large language models to make new things

units.why: The glossary defines LLMs as using "machine learning techniques to help them process language". Definition, P61.
units.anchor: Large language models, or LLMs, use machine learning techniques to help them process language

units.why: The glossary defines machine learning as "a field of computer science, under the umbrella of AI". Definition, P61.
units.anchor: It’s a field of computer science, under the umbrella of AI
units.frag_start: If artificial intelligence is the goal

units.why: The glossary defines hallucinations as "inaccurate responses that developers refer to as hallucinations". Definition, P61 (accuracy duty is coded as P31).
units.anchor: they can give inaccurate responses that developers refer to as hallucinations
units.frag_start: Generative AI systems can create stories

units.why: The glossary defines "Responsible AI" as guiding people "as they try to design systems that are safe and fair". Definition of a term, P61.
units.anchor: Responsible AI guides people as they try to design systems that are safe and fair

units.why: The glossary defines a prompt as "an instruction entered into a system in language, images or code". Definition, P61.
units.anchor: A prompt is an instruction entered into a system in language, images or code

documents.unit: Instructional Design and Delivery (AI in Higher Education)
documents.title: AI Guides and Resources for Faculty
documents.summary: A faculty landing page describing the Faculty AI Use Guide with three value categories, videos on integrity, writing and hallucination, and links to the IT guidelines, library and teaching center. The guide PDF itself is not captured.
documents.stance_why: The page describes a guide sorting AI uses into "High Value," "Some Value," and "Negative Value" and leaves course decisions to instructors; it states no stance of its own.

units.why: "The categories “High Value,” “Some Value,” and “Negative Value” indicate the potential benefit of specific AI uses" defines named categories for classifying AI uses by learning benefit, so P05.
units.anchor: The categories “High Value,” “Some Value,” and “Negative Value”
units.policy: The Faculty AI Use Guide sorts specific AI uses into the categories High Value, Some Value and Negative Value, indicating the potential benefit of each use for student learning.

units.why: "supports instructors in using AI thoughtfully to enhance learning, uphold academic integrity, advance research" says what the guide helps instructors do with AI in their own work, so P59, informing.
units.anchor: supports instructors in using AI thoughtfully to enhance learning, uphold academic integrity
units.frag_start: The guide linked below supports instructors

units.why: "In an AI-driven world, human insight and people-centered education are more valuable than ever" states a principle about the role of human teachers. It is a framing principle, P56.
units.anchor: human insight and people-centered education are more valuable than ever
units.frag_start: In an AI-driven world, human insight

units.why: "Check the CTA Events schedule regularly for AI related training and workshops for faculty" points instructors to AI training, so P63.
units.anchor: Check the CTA Events schedule regularly for AI related training and workshops for faculty.
units.frag_start: The Center for Teaching and Advising

units.why: The Academic Integrity video offers "practical strategies for establishing clear expectations, adapting our pedagogy" to faculty, which is faculty support (P63), not a rule.
units.anchor: offering practical strategies for establishing clear expectations, adapting our pedagogy

units.why: The writing-process video offers "practical strategies for leveraging AI’s strengths to support student learning", including "Socratic tutor bots", to faculty. This is faculty support, P63.
units.anchor: practical strategies for leveraging AI’s strengths to support student learning

units.why: The librarian session provides "the foundational knowledge needed to help students use these tools critically and ethically", which supports faculty learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: the foundational knowledge needed to help students use these tools critically and ethically
units.frag_start: In this presentation, faculty librarian Anthony Tardiff

units.why: "Gonzaga University provides clear guidelines to help faculty and staff navigate the responsible use of artificial intelligence" names the IT guidelines as the institutional framework, P56.
units.anchor: Gonzaga University provides clear guidelines to help faculty and staff navigate the responsible use

notes: The Faculty AI Use Guide PDF (gonzaga.edu/__data/assets/pdf_file/0036/439929/AI-use_letter-size.pdf) is not in Wayback and a direct fetch returned nothing, so only the landing-page summary is captured. No School of Engineering and Applied Science or CS department AI policy found (SEAS pages describe AI programs only).
